name: FRAMES
summary: 824 multi-hop questions written by annotators that need facts from several Wikipedia articles, each with a gold answer and the articles used to answer it.
overview:
FRAMES, the Factuality, Retrieval, And reasoning MEasurement Set, tests retrieval-augmented generation end to end. Each question needs facts from two or more Wikipedia articles, so a system must find the right articles, pull out the relevant facts, and combine them, often with arithmetic, table lookups, or reasoning about dates. The benchmark was released by Google in September 2024. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12941) and [dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/frames-benchmark/blob/58d9fb6330f3ab1316d1eca12e5e8ef23dcc22ef/README.md)

The authors first tried generating questions with a language model, but more than 30% of the generated questions and answers were hallucinated and few needed more than four articles. They instead had expert annotators write questions that combine information from several Wikipedia articles, record the answer and the articles used, and label each question with one or more reasoning types: numerical, tabular, multiple constraints, temporal, and post-processing. Three months later, annotators checked each answer against its articles again and removed 5.5% of the questions whose answers were no longer true. They added dates, such as "As of August 1, 2024", to questions whose answers could change, removed yes-or-no questions, and drew only on Wikipedia. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12941)
methodology:
This snapshot contains all 824 questions in test.tsv at the pinned dataset revision, the dataset's only data file. The upstream labels count 549 questions as multiple constraints, 293 as numerical reasoning, 278 as temporal reasoning, 236 as tabular reasoning, and 107 as post-processing; many questions have more than one. About 38% of questions list two articles, 35% three, and 16% four. The paper and dataset card describe 2 to 15 articles per question, but a few rows list more, up to 23. [Dataset file](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/frames-benchmark/blob/58d9fb6330f3ab1316d1eca12e5e8ef23dcc22ef/test.tsv) and [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12941)

Each Task Prompt is the upstream question verbatim, including the leading or trailing spaces of 67 questions. The Solution is the upstream answer verbatim, a blank line, the label Wikipedia articles:, and the question's article links, one upstream cell per line in column order. Most answers are short names, numbers, or phrases; some are sentences or short paragraphs, and question 324's answer is a 1,360-character summary with Markdown bold markers. Questions 52, 107, and 108 have Yes or No answers, although the paper says yes-or-no questions were removed. The reasoning-type labels and the wiki_links column, which repeats the link cells as a list, are not stored.

The link cells are kept as published. The file has ten link columns and an overflow column; in eight questions the overflow cell holds several comma-separated links, and questions 8 and 90 leave some of the ten columns empty before it. Most links point to English Wikipedia articles. Eleven questions use mobile en.m.wikipedia.org links, fifteen use links with a #:~:text= fragment that highlights a passage, and question 823 links to Simple English Wikipedia. Question 88 links to a Wikipedia search, question 98 to a redirect page, question 226 gives links without https://, question 495 uses a w.wiki short link, and question 644 notes that one article is not required but helpful. Links point to current articles rather than the revisions the annotators read.

The source has no question IDs beyond its zero-based row index. IDs are question- followed by that index as three digits, such as question-000. Prompt and solution source links point to the pinned data file, which has no per-question links. No task-specific software environment is required. The importer uses only Python's standard library and can be rerun with python3 data/frames/import.py.
scoring:
Answers are free-form text, so the paper grades them with a language model. The rater sees the question, the model's response, and the gold answer, and decides whether the meaning and vital facts of the gold answer appear in the response, explaining its decision before giving TRUE or FALSE. With Gemini-Pro-1.5-0514 as the rater, its decisions agreed with human judgments with an accuracy of 0.96 and a Cohen's kappa of 0.889. The score is the fraction of questions judged correct. The dataset release includes no evaluation code; the paper gives the rater prompt. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12941)

The paper reports results in several settings: the question alone, the question with the top 2 or 4 articles retrieved by BM25 from a Wikipedia dump, the question with the text of all its gold articles, and a multi-step pipeline in which the model writes search queries over several rounds of BM25 retrieval. Gemini-Pro-1.5-0514 scored 0.408 with the question alone, 0.452 and 0.474 with two and four retrieved articles, 0.729 with the gold articles, and up to 0.66 with the multi-step pipeline. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12941) and [dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/frames-benchmark/blob/58d9fb6330f3ab1316d1eca12e5e8ef23dcc22ef/README.md)

Compare results that use the same setting, the same retrieval corpus, and the same rater model and prompt. Benchopedia stores the questions, gold answers, and article links. It does not run evaluations or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
The paper notes that the facts come from Wikipedia, which is widely used in training data, so models may have seen the information, and that the questions may not represent the full range of real queries. Questions that need arithmetic or other operations reduce, but do not remove, the benefit of memorized facts. The questions were written in English from English Wikipedia. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12941)

Wikipedia changes over time. The annotators dated some questions and removed ones whose answers had changed within three months, but other answers may since have become outdated, and the linked articles may no longer contain the facts the annotators used. Scores from a language-model rater depend on the rater model and prompt, and the rater can disagree with human judges. With 824 questions in a single test set, small differences in accuracy may not be meaningful. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12941)
